h: The story of a very special stone
p: Blue John has been prized for centuries, and in the 18th and 19th centuries it was turned into vases, bowls and decorative pieces for grand country houses. Its name is something of a puzzle. One popular theory says it comes from the French "bleu-jaune", meaning blue-yellow, a nod to the stone's colours, though nobody can say for certain. Either way, seeing the veins in their natural setting gives you a new respect for anyone who mined it by candlelight.

Inside, look out for how the colours shift from deep purple to amber as the light catches the rock. Your guide will point out the best examples, and it's well worth asking questions; the guides tend to know the cavern inside out and love sharing the old mining stories.

Plan around the climb. The steps are fine for most reasonably fit people, but take your time on the way back up, and keep a close eye on younger children on the wetter sections. Allow a bit of extra time either side of the tour to get your breath back and enjoy the views over the valley.

The location is a cracker for walkers. The cavern sits at the foot of Mam Tor, near the old main road that was abandoned after landslips broke it apart, and the cracked, tilted tarmac makes for a fascinating walk. Winnats Pass, a dramatic limestone gorge, is just round the corner too.
Combine the cavern with a visit to Treak Cliff, Castleton's other Blue John cave, and you'll go home knowing more about this little stone than most geologists.
